correctness.rationale: Any two compatible placements specify two distinct input-output assignments of a permutation of three letters, so they belong to just one full permutation block, which also contains any third compatible placement extending them. Each vertex alone occurs in two blocks; two distinct permutations meet in n vertices iff they differ by a transposition. The nine intersecting pairs form K_{3,3}, with n distinct identifications per pair. All blocks are connected: given two rook positions in Δ_{3,n}, choose a row and column avoiding the row and column of both. To check the gluing, replace identifications by intervals in the disjoint union of the blocks. The intervals are disjoint because each block-slot vertex is used once, so each can be collapsed as a contractible CW subcomplex; the quotient recovers X_n up to homotopy. Instead one can move the endpoint attaching maps to chosen block basepoints by paths (homotopy invariance of the graph-of-spaces attachment), then contract a spanning tree. The resulting wedge has six blocks and 9n−5 circles; the decomposition is not a canonical choice of based wedge maps. At n=3 every edge belongs to a unique triangle, so one distinct free edge can be removed per triangle; the graph has 9 vertices and 12 edges, giving 4 circles per block. At n=4 vertex links are K_{3,3} minus a matching (six-cycles), and adjacent triangles swap the appended unused column with one row column, giving opposite orientations along their shared edge. The connected orientable surface has Euler characteristic 0, hence is a torus. For n≥5, BLVZ Theorem 1.1 makes each ordinary block simply connected. The rank of its free H₂ is χ−1=3n−3n(n−1)+n(n−1)(n−2)−1; Hurewicz and homological Whitehead give the claimed two-sphere wedge. These checks yield 46 circles at n=3, six tori and 31 extra circles at n=4, the sphere/circle formulas thereafter, and the fundamental groups and torsion-free integral homology. Read the bundled finite checker, not run; no inference from finite-field ranks to integer homology is needed.

evidence: The first two sizes are 3,3, so BLVZ Theorem 3.1 gives a connectivity parameter ν=2 and does not give simple connectivity. Proposition 3.4 gives an ordinary-board homology summand via a coordinate projection with a section. Athanasiadis Theorem 3.2 uses ν=min(n_1−1,⌊(n_1+n_2−2)/3⌋), which is 1 here; his general theorem gives connectedness and a vertex-decomposable 1-skeleton, not decomposition of the two-dimensional complex.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Even a sharp connectivity bound does not fix a nonzero fundamental group's rank or presentation or the full homotopy type of these boards. A split homology inclusion for one ordinary board is not an identification of six entire factors and their vertex gluing.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Unlike the inspected general theorems, the audited proof identifies the intersection graph as K_{3,3} and exactly n point-identifications per edge. These data give the free factor F_{9n−5} even when each block is simply connected. The graph-matching and avoidance statements cannot specialize to these incidences or their homotopy pushout, regardless of catalog date.

evidence: BLVZ define the multidimensional complex by avoiding repeated coordinates. Equivalently it is the clique complex of the categorical product of K_3, K_3 and K_n. A graph matching complex on the ordinary Cartesian grid instead has grid edges as vertices; neither its faces nor its graph product agree.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: An indexed grid or tripartite graph result is equivalent only if its face condition translates to this three-coordinate rule, not merely because the dimensions or side sizes agree. The primary multidimensional definition does translate, so its results were compared directly.

exact_database_or_table.reasoning: The known small-board torus belongs to an ordinary block; the six-factor decomposition and the 31 extra circles at n=4 are assertions about a different complex. No exact matching three-way classification was found in the inspected indexed comparisons; search absence alone does not establish novelty.

originality.rationale: The supported distinct statement is the gluing and full homotopy type of the three-coordinate (3,3,n) matching complex, not the connectivity or types of the ordinary two-coordinate blocks. The directly checked general multidimensional results give connectedness and an ordinary-board homology summand, not the six factors and additional fundamental group. Related indexed ordinary graph matching/avoidance results are different functors on different objects.
residual_risks: A decomposition published under hypergraph matching or categorical product terminology could escape these bounded comparisons.
The nonequivariant result does not classify all coordinate-permutation actions; no canonical based splitting or priority ordering among same-day records is asserted.

value.rationale: This natural small-side infinite family has an exact, integral homotopy classification, not merely a connectivity bound or table of ranks. The block graph explains why the fundamental group is nontrivial at arbitrarily large n even though each ordinary block is simply connected, and why there are genuine torus summands at n=4. That gives structural information of independent use when testing broader multidimensional chessboard claims.
